title: President Names Jay Clayton to Lead New White House AI Group
summary:
President Donald Trump said on Sunday that Jay Clayton is the new White House "AI czar." Clayton is the director of national intelligence. Trump announced the news on Truth Social. He said Clayton will lead a new group called the "Super Intelligence Force." Trump wrote that the group will "ensure that America continues to lead the World in Super Intelligence." Trump prefers the term "super intelligence" to "artificial intelligence."

According to Trump, the group will coordinate the federal government's work with consumers, public interest groups, religious organizations, companies that run important systems like power and water, and super intelligence companies. Trump also named other members. They are Federal Trade Commission Chairman Andrew Ferguson, Office of Personnel Management Director Scott Kupor, and Emil Michael, a defense department official in charge of research and engineering.

The announcement follows warnings from some tech leaders about the risks of fast-moving AI, including worries that it could go rogue. Trump has largely brushed those warnings aside. On Tuesday, he met with AI company leaders at the White House. He said several of them signed a voluntary agreement that includes reviews of their work from inside and outside their companies. This week the White House also launched a new website, America.gov, which says its content is gathered by AI from official government sources.

It is unclear what Clayton's new job will mean for the AI industry. Rules from the U.S. government are limited, and Congress has not passed a broad law about AI. Some states, including California, have rules, such as requiring that people be told when AI is used. Last month Clayton told CNBC that super intelligence is a national security issue. He also disagreed with calls to pause AI development, noting that other countries are continuing their work.
why_it_matters: The article shows how the U.S. government is organizing its work on AI while rules are limited, and why people are still debating how fast AI should develop.
